title: 04 - Equality

content.text: Syllabus — Equality: social, political and economic; relationship between equality and freedom; affirmative action. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 4)

Q — Trace the historical evolution and meaning of equality, and compare the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner.
Three tasks — how equality became a political demand, what it actually means, and how the three thinkers define it.

(Caste rank was defended as the divinely ordained order until the social reformers attacked it.)
— the concept is defined twice over:
— the opportunity to develop one’s personality.
— ‘the will of one is equal to the will of any other’.
— above all education, the power to use knowledge.
— economic equality is ‘a problem of proportion’, not identical incomes but a defensible spread.
value, flowing from the development of personality.
(Whatever right is guaranteed to me must be guaranteed to you in the same measure.)
— an open entrance exam on merit.
— equal coaching, nutrition and schooling before it.
— equality matures from a negative demand (Laski) to a developmental ideal (Barker) to a graded modern typology (Turner).

Inequality — by ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ — was for most of history treated as natural and therefore beyond criticism, as caste rank was defended in India as a divinely ordained order. The

J.S. Mill, T.H. Green and Marx
The concept is defined twice over, and because the two faces pull in different directions equality remains an
— it is the end of special privileges, so that no one may claim advantage by birth — the logic of abolishing untouchability.
— it is the availability to each person of the opportunity to develop his or her personality — the logic of free schooling and mid-day meals.

— for all, especially education, ‘for the power that counts is the power to use knowledge’.

— ‘derivative from the supreme value of the development of personality’. Its operative rule is reciprocity: “whatever rights are guaranteed to me shall also, and in the same measure, be guaranteed to others.” Equality is thus justified instrumentally, by what it enables each personality to become.

— of persons, that is equal human dignity and worth.
— open access on merit and talent, as in a competitive entrance examination.

— or result, which equalises end-states through law.

Read together, the three show equality maturing from a negative demand (Laski’s end of privilege) to a positive, developmental ideal (Barker’s personality) and finally to a graded modern typology (Turner) that sets up the central debate between opportunity and outcome.
Q — “Equality of outcome, though the most radical face of egalitarianism, threatens liberty.” Critically examine, distinguishing formal equality, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome.
Separate the three forms of equality, then judge whether the most radical of them — outcome — destroys liberty.
— ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’, and the demand rises in three stages.
(Same law → same starting line → same finishing line.)
— ‘all men are created equal’: equality before law, but essentially
(An equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant is worthless if you cannot pay the bill; the queue rule ‘first come, first served’ is fair but blind to need.)
— ‘an equal chance to become unequal’: strip away social handicaps, accept natural difference.
(No child should start the race halfway down the track — hence free schooling and mid-day meals before the entrance exam.)
: ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’.
(Not an equal chance at the seat, but an equal share of the harvest.)
— the charge and its answer stand opposed:
— people differ, so equal treatment must yield inequality; outcome equality needs coercive social engineering and kills incentive.
— treating unequals equally is itself unjust, so differential treatment is the price of real equality.
— formal equality is free but hollow, outcome equality deep but coercive;
difference principle is offered as the mean.

Egalitarianism rests on the presumption that ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’ — the burden of proof lies on whoever defends a difference. On that premise equality has assumed three progressively radical forms, each demanding more of the state: the same law, then the same starting line, then the same finishing line.

Formal or legal equality asserts a common human essence — ‘all men are created equal’ (US Declaration), ‘men are born free and equal in rights’ (French Declaration) — and is expressed as equality before law, the cornerstone of the

: it grants an equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant while ignoring whether one has the money, and leaves ‘institutionalised’ discrimination untouched. In the queue, ‘first come, first served’ is impeccably fair and wholly insensitive to need.

and amounts to ‘an equal opportunity to become unequal’: natural inequality of talent and effort is accepted, while social inequality of poverty and poor schooling is removed, so that no one ‘starts the race halfway down the track’. It is the tenet of
, realised through education, health and housing — free schooling and mid-day meals precede the common entrance examination.
Equality of outcome is ‘the most radical and controversial face of egalitarianism’ — not an equal start but an equal finish, so that ‘all runners finish in line together’.
feared that inequality would enslave the poor and corrupt the rich, and
captured the ideal in ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’ — distribution keyed to need rather than to contribution or to chance.
The charge that outcome equality destroys freedom, and its answer, stand opposed:

— ‘people are very different, so to treat them equally must result in inequality — the only way to make them equal is to treat them differently’; equality of outcome therefore requires coercive ‘social engineering’, destroys incentive and ‘remains utopia’.

— ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but when unequals are treated equally’ — so a measure of differential treatment is the price of real equality, not an assault on freedom.

The three forms trade off against liberty differently: formal equality is fully compatible with liberty but hollow; equality of opportunity is the liberal mean; equality of outcome secures the deepest equality but at the cost of coercion — which is why
difference principle, permitting only those inequalities that benefit the least advantaged, is offered as the balance between the two extremes.
Q — Critically examine the schools of thought on equality — liberal (welfare, resources, capability), Marxist, communitarian and multiculturalist.
Compare four schools by asking each the same question — equality of WHAT, and among whom.
— liberals agree on equality but differ on what to equalise:
(Equal cash to a healthy man and a dialysis patient is equal resources, not equal welfare.)
compensates what you did not choose, not what you did:
— born with a disability or into a caste; compensated.
— losing money on a bet freely taken; not compensated.
: equalise ‘the ability to do what one wants’, since people convert resources differently.
(‘Fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — same empty stomach, opposite freedoms.)
: ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production.
— equality relocated in spheres and cultures:
blocks advantage in one sphere from buying another.
(Wealth may buy a car, it must not buy a medical seat or a verdict.)
— the schools move outward from the individual to the group, showing genuine equality is plural, not simple.
Liberals agree that persons must be treated as equals but divide over the ‘currency’ of equality:
— the utilitarian answer, which equates welfare with pleasure and would transfer resources until satisfactions are level — which rewards expensive tastes.
, rejects welfare for resources, holding that ‘equality is more fundamental than liberty — liberty is hollow without it’.
holds people responsible only for choices made in
ones, and therefore insists on a
: his ‘envy test’ and his ambition- and endowment-sensitive auction distinguish two kinds of luck, the aim being a distribution that is ‘equitable, not merely equal’:
— the disability or the caste one is born into, which must be compensated.
— the loss on a wager freely taken, which must not.

— ‘the ability to do what one wants to do’ — because individuals differ in converting identical resources into actual functionings: the same grain feeds a healthy adult and fails a parasite-ridden child. The approach is social-choice based and realization-focused, and its sharpest formulation is that ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — the outcome is identical, the freedom is not. Hence development is itself ‘freedom’.

makes the abolition of classes central — ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — which is impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production. Legal and political equality alone is a bourgeois form: so long as one class owns the productive apparatus, formal equality of rights merely legitimises substantive domination.
Both schools relocate equality beyond the individual:

: ‘sometimes we equalise people by differentiating’, and each social good — money, office, health, honour — has its own distributive sphere, so that advantage in one must be blocked from buying advantage in another. Wealth may legitimately buy a car; it must not buy a medical seat or a favourable verdict.
relocate equality in cultures and demand
, Kymlicka’s ‘luck egalitarianism’ treating birth into a minority culture as ‘bad brute luck’ deserving special protection.

The schools move outward from the individual to the group: liberals refine what each person should have (welfare → resources → capability), Marxists locate equality in the abolition of class, and communitarians and multiculturalists relocate it in spheres and cultures — together showing that genuine equality is plural, not simple.
Q — Discuss the dimensions of equality — legal, political, economic and social — and how they combine into formal and substantive equality.
List the four working dimensions of equality, then show which two make ‘formal’ equality and which two make ‘substantive’ equality.
— rule of law plus ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.
(Equal rights are useless without equal power to vindicate them — hence free legal aid.)
— ‘one person, one vote’ with no bar to office; yet
: ‘the many have always been governed by the few’.
(Every vote weighs the same, but money, birth and bureaucracy still weigh more.)
— a level playing field of access to wealth;
: it needs ‘the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’.
(Progressive taxation funding schools and health — Laski’s ‘problem of proportion’.)
— ends discrimination by caste, creed, religion or sex, and is ‘enhanced by affirmative action’.
(Temple entry and common water sources, not merely an equal wage.)
— the four dimensions combine into two.
(A separate line for the elderly and the disabled.)
— the welfare state’s task is to convert formal equality into substantive equality.
Legal equality grants equal legal status to all: the
, supplemented by ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.

regarded it as the primary mark of an equal society. Its limit is decisive: it is ‘meaningless without equal opportunity to get justice — all may possess equal rights but not equal power to vindicate them’, which is why free legal aid, not merely an open court, is required.
Political equality means equal political rights on a ‘one person, one vote’ basis, with no bar of birth or property to holding office.
nevertheless notes that the ‘many have always been governed by the few’: political inequality has rested successively on knowledge (
), birth (aristocracy), money (plutocracy) and race, and real power may still vest in the bureaucracy, police and army rather than in the electorate.
Economic equality seeks a ‘level playing field’ of access to wealth and the means of livelihood.
insists that ‘equality of opportunity is not simply legal equality — it depends on the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’, so the state must actively build capacity.
adds that it is ‘a problem of proportion’, met through differential taxation and social expenditure rather than identical incomes.

Social equality ends discrimination on grounds of caste, creed, religion, sex and the like, attacking status hierarchy rather than income — the equal use of a temple, a well or a school matters as much as the equal wage. It is the dimension most resistant to legislation alone, which is why it is said to be ‘enhanced by affirmative action’.
The four dimensions combine into two composite forms, and the queue captures the difference exactly:
”; ‘first come, first served’ applies one rule to everybody.
”; a separate line for the elderly or the differently-abled relaxes the rule according to need.

Formal equality supplies equal rules and equal votes; substantive equality supplies real, need-sensitive equality of condition — and the central task of the modern welfare state is to convert the former into the latter.
Q — “Affirmative action is indispensable to substantive equality yet deeply contested.” Examine the arguments for and against it, with the Indian reservation debate.
Define affirmative action, argue both sides, and settle the Indian reservation question with the courts’ test.
— ‘positive intervention by the state’ in favour of the historically disadvantaged.
(Reservation for SCs/STs in India, affirmative action for Blacks in the USA.)
— the unit of claim is the community, not the person.
(A poor Brahmin does not qualify, since his community suffered no historical disadvantage — he is helped by poverty schemes instead.)
— it is the engine that turns formal equality into substantive equality:
— on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’, correcting unjust historical inequality.
— the already advantaged within a beneficiary group edge out poorer members of the majority.
— the present generation is ‘not responsible for past injustice’.
— breeding a feeling of inferiority in those it is meant to lift.
— indispensable, but legitimate only while it stays targeted, time-bound and evidence-based.
Affirmative action is ‘positive intervention by the state — welfare policies in favour of the disadvantaged’. It targets the

— Dalits and Adivasis in India, Blacks in the United States — and works by relaxing a uniform rule (reserved seats, relaxed cut-offs, preferential appointment) so that those excluded for centuries can in fact enter. It must be distinguished from a mere
secured by already dominant groups, such as the Jat and Maratha agitations.
Its unit of claim is the
class or community, not the individual

. A poor Brahmin does not qualify, because his community suffered no historical disadvantage — his poverty is addressed instead by income-based poverty-alleviation schemes. This is what distinguishes affirmative action from welfare simpliciter: it remedies a status injury inflicted on a group, not a shortfall of income suffered by a person.
It is the engine by which formal equality is converted into substantive equality, and the case rests on two limbs:
— positive discrimination on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’, correcting
and enabling the deprived to ‘escape tough competition’ in which their starting handicap would be decisive.
— in India it is grounded in
, which permit special provision for socially and educationally backward classes.

’, since already advantaged members of a beneficiary group may edge out poorer members of the majority.
— the present generation is ‘not responsible for past injustice’, so the burden falls in the wrong place.
, breeding a ‘feeling of inferiority’ in those it is meant to lift.
Critics and courts have framed the Indian question in three voices:
observes that reservation debates ‘generate more heat than light’.
case the government was directed to keep identifying genuinely vulnerable classes on fresh evidence rather than political pressure, and in
it was held that reservation is ‘the medicine, not the daily bread’ — a remedy for a diagnosed disability, not a permanent diet.
Affirmative action is indispensable for converting formal into substantive equality, and is simply
rule that unequals be treated unequally. Its legitimacy, however, depends on its remaining
— correcting a historical wrong without hardening into a permanent entitlement.
Q — Is liberty a precondition for equality? Examine the relationship between liberty, equality and justice, and evaluate Berlin’s value pluralism.
Take the liberty–equality relation through three schools, then test whether Berlin’s pluralism allows any final ranking.
— liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’, and three schools read the relation differently.
(Does a quota that opens a college seat enlarge freedom or invade it?)
: the two are contradictory, so liberty comes first and equality stops at law and opportunity.
(Redistribution means taxing one man to fund another.)
— equality first, since ‘bourgeois’ liberty is a privilege of the propertied;
: ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’.
(A literate voter is a freer voter.)
— lexical order: equal basic liberties first, the difference principle after.
— values are ‘plural, conflicting and incommensurable’, with no objective ordering.
(The goods of the nun’s life and the married woman’s are both real and cannot both be had.)
— liberty is a precondition only for
equality — ‘treating people as equals’; justice remains the balancing value.

Liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’ values, and the practical form of the dispute is sharp: does a reserved seat or a redistributive tax enlarge the freedom of the excluded, or invade the freedom of the taxed? Three schools answer differently, according to whether they treat the two values as contradictory, as hierarchically ordered, or as mutually completing.
) hold liberty and equality to be
, give liberty priority, and confine equality to legal equality and equality of opportunity, since redistribution means coercing one person for another’s benefit.
: ‘people are very different, so treating them equally must produce inequality; equality before law leads to material inequality’ — a result he accepts as the price of freedom.

Socialists and Marxists reverse the order: equality trumps a merely ‘bourgeois’ liberty, because without material equality freedom is the privilege of the propertied — the right to own a newspaper means nothing to one who cannot buy one.
states the point decisively: ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’.
) deny any necessary conflict, by three distinct routes:
, the equal basic liberties ranking first and the difference principle governing what remains.
— he does so through endowment- and ambition-sensitive distribution.

— through ‘development as freedom’, since literacy, health and nutrition are what make a formal right usable. On this view liberty, properly understood, is a precondition of a meaningful equal life, not its enemy.

argues that fundamental values are ‘universal, plural, conflicting and incommensurable’ — ‘there is no objective criterion to determine their ordering’, as the goods realised in the life of a nun and in that of a married woman are both genuine and cannot both be possessed. He rejects value monism, which assumes one true ranking, and equally value relativism, which denies that values are real: liberty and equality are both authentic goods that may irreducibly clash.
Liberty is a precondition for equality only when equality is understood
— as ‘treating people as equals’ with equal concern and respect, rather than treating them identically.
pluralism warns that no single formula can always harmonise them, which is precisely why justice, as the balancing value, remains the central task of political theory.
Q — “Aristotle supports proportionate, not absolute, equality.” Discuss his conception of equality and its relevance to modern substantive equality.
Explain what proportional equality means in Aristotle, note its limits in his own society, and show it is the logic of affirmative action today.
: ‘the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’.
(Equal marks deserve equal grades; unequal need deserves unequal help.)
— ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’.
(One flight of stairs for everyone is equal treatment that excludes the wheelchair user.)
— in distributive justice, honours and wealth go by relevant merit, not identical division; hence
— proportionality is only as just as its criteria of relevance:
— he ranked citizens above slaves and men above women in ‘rational and civic capacity’.
— ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’.
— ‘unequals treated unequally’ is the very logic of
— for the disabled, and a separate queue for the elderly — all relax a uniform rule for the disadvantaged.
— though framed in a hierarchical Greek polis, his proportionality is the enduring premise of the welfare state.

he defines just equality as “the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” Equality is thus a ratio, not a quantity: what is owed to a person depends on the relevant respect in which he stands equal or unequal to others, so identical treatment is just only among genuine equals.

From this follows his most quoted proposition: ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’. The second half is the radical half — a single flight of stairs applied to everyone alike is impeccably equal treatment which nonetheless excludes the person in a wheelchair. Uniformity, in other words, can itself be a form of injustice.
Equality therefore becomes a matter of

: in distributive justice, honours, office and wealth are to be shared according to relevant merit rather than divided identically, and the argument turns on which respects are relevant to which good. He accordingly rejects
as itself a source of injustice — the objection later pressed by
Proportionality is only as just as the criteria of relevance it employs, and Aristotle’s own criteria were severely limited:

— he distinguished citizens from slaves and men from women in ‘rational and civic capacity’, restricted participation in the Polis to citizens, and even held slavery to be ‘good for both master and slave’.
— he was acutely alert to inequality’s dangers: ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’.
His principle that ‘unequals be treated unequally’ is precisely the logic of modern
, each instance relaxing a uniform rule in favour of the disadvantaged:
— under Articles 15 and 16 of the Indian Constitution.
— unequal rates levied on unequal incomes.
— special provisions for the disabled and a separate queue for the elderly, treating unequals unequally so as to produce genuine rather than merely formal equality.

Aristotle’s proportional equality, though embedded in a hierarchical Greek society, supplies the enduring insight behind today’s welfare state — that real equality often requires differential, need-sensitive treatment rather than identical treatment for all.

(UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 4) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning and evolution of equality (formal, of opportunity, of outcome); the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner; the schools of thought (liberal — welfare/resources/capability, Marxist, communitarian, multiculturalist); the dimensions of equality (legal, political, economic, social); affirmative action; and the relation of equality with liberty and justice, including Berlin’s value pluralism. Must-know thinkers:  Laski, Barker, Bryan Turner, Aristotle, Rousseau, Marx, Engels, Hayek, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum, Michael Walzer, Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, R.H. Tawney, Hobhouse, Isaiah Berlin, Rawls. PYQ trend:  equality of outcome, Aristotle’s conception, affirmative action, the liberty–equality relationship, and Berlin’s value pluralism are the recurring themes. Master Questions Q — Trace the historical evolution and meaning of equality, and compare the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner. What it’s asking:  Three tasks — how equality became a political demand, what it actually means, and how the three thinkers define it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Evolution  — inequality of ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ was long thought natural, until the  Renaissance, Reformation and natural-rights theory  made equality a demand.  (Caste rank was defended as the divinely ordained order until the social reformers attacked it.) 2. Meaning  — the concept is defined twice over:    2.1 Negatively  — the end of special privilege.  (Abolishing untouchability.)    2.2 Positively  — the opportunity to develop one’s personality.  (Free schooling and mid-day meals.) 3. Laski  — four elements of equality:    3.1 No special privilege  — ‘the will of one is equal to the will of any other’.    3.2 Adequate opportunity  — above all education, the power to use knowledge.    3.3 Access to social benefits  — with no bar of birth.    3.4 No exploitation  — economic equality is ‘a problem of proportion’, not identical incomes but a defensible spread. 4. Barker  — equality is a  derivative  value, flowing from the development of personality.  (Whatever right is guaranteed to me must be guaranteed to you in the same measure.) 5. Turner  — four types of equality:    5.1 Fundamental equality  — equal human dignity and worth.    5.2 Equality of opportunity  — an open entrance exam on merit.    5.3 Equality of condition  — equal coaching, nutrition and schooling before it.    5.4 Equality of outcome  — an equal result after it. 6. Conclusion  — equality matures from a negative demand (Laski) to a developmental ideal (Barker) to a graded modern typology (Turner). Model Answer 1. Evolution.  Inequality — by ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ — was for most of history treated as natural and therefore beyond criticism, as caste rank was defended in India as a divinely ordained order. The  Renaissance, Reformation and natural-rights theory  — pre-eminently  Locke  — turned equality into a political demand, directed first against feudal and clerical privilege and then, in the nineteenth century, extended to  economic and social equality  by  J.S. Mill, T.H. Green and Marx . 2. Meaning.  The concept is defined twice over, and because the two faces pull in different directions equality remains an  ‘essentially contested concept’ :    2.1 Negatively  — it is the end of special privileges, so that no one may claim advantage by birth — the logic of abolishing untouchability.    2.2 Positively  — it is the availability to each person of the opportunity to develop his or her personality — the logic of free schooling and mid-day meals. 3. Laski.  Harold Laski  defines equality through four elements:    3.1 No special privilege  — ‘the will of one is equal to the will of any other’.    3.2 Adequate opportunity  — for all, especially education, ‘for the power that counts is the power to use knowledge’.    3.3 Access to social benefits  — with no bar of birth.    3.4 No exploitation  — the absence of economic and social exploitation; on the economic side he concedes it is ‘largely a problem of proportion’, not of identical incomes. 4. Barker.  Ernest Barker  treats equality not as an end in itself but as a  derivative value  — ‘derivative from the supreme value of the development of personality’. Its operative rule is reciprocity: “whatever rights are guaranteed to me shall also, and in the same measure, be guaranteed to others.” Equality is thus justified instrumentally, by what it enables each personality to become. 5. Turner.  Bryan Turner  (in  Equality ) gives the most comprehensive modern account, distinguishing four types:    5.1 Fundamental equality  — of persons, that is equal human dignity and worth.    5.2 Equality of opportunity  — open access on merit and talent, as in a competitive entrance examination.    5.3 Equality of condition  — which equalises the starting points, the coaching, nutrition and schooling that precede the exam.    5.4 Equality of outcome  — or result, which equalises end-states through law. 6. Conclusion.  Read together, the three show equality maturing from a negative demand (Laski’s end of privilege) to a positive, developmental ideal (Barker’s personality) and finally to a graded modern typology (Turner) that sets up the central debate between opportunity and outcome. Q — “Equality of outcome, though the most radical face of egalitarianism, threatens liberty.” Critically examine, distinguishing formal equality, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome. What it’s asking:  Separate the three forms of equality, then judge whether the most radical of them — outcome — destroys liberty. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Egalitarian premise  — ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’, and the demand rises in three stages.  (Same law → same starting line → same finishing line.) 2. Formal equality  — ‘all men are created equal’: equality before law, but essentially  negative .  (An equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant is worthless if you cannot pay the bill; the queue rule ‘first come, first served’ is fair but blind to need.) 3. Equality of opportunity  — ‘an equal chance to become unequal’: strip away social handicaps, accept natural difference.  (No child should start the race halfway down the track — hence free schooling and mid-day meals before the entrance exam.) 4. Equality of outcome  — ‘all runners finish in line together’;  Marx : ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’.  (Not an equal chance at the seat, but an equal share of the harvest.) 5. Threat to liberty  — the charge and its answer stand opposed:    5.1 Hayek’s objection  — people differ, so equal treatment must yield inequality; outcome equality needs coercive social engineering and kills incentive.    5.2 Aristotle’s reply  — treating unequals equally is itself unjust, so differential treatment is the price of real equality. 6. Conclusion  — formal equality is free but hollow, outcome equality deep but coercive;  Rawls’  difference principle is offered as the mean. Model Answer 1. Egalitarian premise.  Egalitarianism rests on the presumption that ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’ — the burden of proof lies on whoever defends a difference. On that premise equality has assumed three progressively radical forms, each demanding more of the state: the same law, then the same starting line, then the same finishing line. 2. Formal equality.  Formal or legal equality asserts a common human essence — ‘all men are created equal’ (US Declaration), ‘men are born free and equal in rights’ (French Declaration) — and is expressed as equality before law, the cornerstone of the  rule of law . Yet it is  essentially negative : it grants an equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant while ignoring whether one has the money, and leaves ‘institutionalised’ discrimination untouched. In the queue, ‘first come, first served’ is impeccably fair and wholly insensitive to need. 3. Equality of opportunity.  Proportional equality, traceable to  Plato , concerns  starting conditions  and amounts to ‘an equal opportunity to become unequal’: natural inequality of talent and effort is accepted, while social inequality of poverty and poor schooling is removed, so that no one ‘starts the race halfway down the track’. It is the tenet of  social liberalism , realised through education, health and housing — free schooling and mid-day meals precede the common entrance examination. 4. Equality of outcome.  Equality of outcome is ‘the most radical and controversial face of egalitarianism’ — not an equal start but an equal finish, so that ‘all runners finish in line together’.  Rousseau  feared that inequality would enslave the poor and corrupt the rich, and  Marx  captured the ideal in ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’ — distribution keyed to need rather than to contribution or to chance. 5. Threat to liberty.  The charge that outcome equality destroys freedom, and its answer, stand opposed:    5.1 Hayek’s objection  — ‘people are very different, so to treat them equally must result in inequality — the only way to make them equal is to treat them differently’; equality of outcome therefore requires coercive ‘social engineering’, destroys incentive and ‘remains utopia’.    5.2 Aristotle’s reply  — ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but when unequals are treated equally’ — so a measure of differential treatment is the price of real equality, not an assault on freedom. 6. Conclusion.  The three forms trade off against liberty differently: formal equality is fully compatible with liberty but hollow; equality of opportunity is the liberal mean; equality of outcome secures the deepest equality but at the cost of coercion — which is why  Rawls’  difference principle, permitting only those inequalities that benefit the least advantaged, is offered as the balance between the two extremes. Q — Critically examine the schools of thought on equality — liberal (welfare, resources, capability), Marxist, communitarian and multiculturalist. What it’s asking:  Compare four schools by asking each the same question — equality of WHAT, and among whom. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The currency question  — liberals agree on equality but differ on what to equalise:    1.1 Equality of welfare  — the utilitarian answer, levelling satisfactions.    1.2 Equality of resources  —  Dworkin ,  Sovereign Virtue .  (Equal cash to a healthy man and a dialysis patient is equal resources, not equal welfare.) 2. Brute luck vs option luck  —  Dworkin  compensates what you did not choose, not what you did:    2.1 Brute luck  — born with a disability or into a caste; compensated.    2.2 Option luck  — losing money on a bet freely taken; not compensated. 3. Capability  —  Sen  and  Nussbaum : equalise ‘the ability to do what one wants’, since people convert resources differently.  (‘Fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — same empty stomach, opposite freedoms.) 4. Marxist  —  Marx : ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production. 5. Communitarian & multiculturalist  — equality relocated in spheres and cultures:    5.1 Communitarian  —  Walzer’s   complex equality  blocks advantage in one sphere from buying another.  (Wealth may buy a car, it must not buy a medical seat or a verdict.)    5.2 Multiculturalist  —  Kymlicka  and  Parekh  demand group rights. 6. Conclusion  — the schools move outward from the individual to the group, showing genuine equality is plural, not simple. Model Answer 1. The currency question.  Liberals agree that persons must be treated as equals but divide over the ‘currency’ of equality:    1.1 Equality of welfare  — the utilitarian answer, which equates welfare with pleasure and would transfer resources until satisfactions are level — which rewards expensive tastes.    1.2 Equality of resources  —  Ronald Dworkin , in  Sovereign Virtue , rejects welfare for resources, holding that ‘equality is more fundamental than liberty — liberty is hollow without it’. 2. Brute luck versus option luck.  Dworkin  holds people responsible only for choices made in  chosen  circumstances, not  unchosen  ones, and therefore insists on a  just initial distribution : his ‘envy test’ and his ambition- and endowment-sensitive auction distinguish two kinds of luck, the aim being a distribution that is ‘equitable, not merely equal’:    2.1 Brute luck  — the disability or the caste one is born into, which must be compensated.    2.2 Option luck  — the loss on a wager freely taken, which must not. 3. Capability.  Amartya Sen , refined by  Martha Nussbaum , urges  equality of capability  — ‘the ability to do what one wants to do’ — because individuals differ in converting identical resources into actual functionings: the same grain feeds a healthy adult and fails a parasite-ridden child. The approach is social-choice based and realization-focused, and its sharpest formulation is that ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — the outcome is identical, the freedom is not. Hence development is itself ‘freedom’. 4. Marxist.  Marx  makes the abolition of classes central — ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — which is impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production. Legal and political equality alone is a bourgeois form: so long as one class owns the productive apparatus, formal equality of rights merely legitimises substantive domination. 5. Communitarian and multiculturalist.  Both schools relocate equality beyond the individual:    5.1 Communitarian  —  Michael Walzer  argues for  complex equality : ‘sometimes we equalise people by differentiating’, and each social good — money, office, health, honour — has its own distributive sphere, so that advantage in one must be blocked from buying advantage in another. Wealth may legitimately buy a car; it must not buy a medical seat or a favourable verdict.    5.2 Multiculturalist  —  Will Kymlicka  and  Bhikhu Parekh  relocate equality in cultures and demand  group rights , Kymlicka’s ‘luck egalitarianism’ treating birth into a minority culture as ‘bad brute luck’ deserving special protection. 6. Conclusion.  The schools move outward from the individual to the group: liberals refine what each person should have (welfare → resources → capability), Marxists locate equality in the abolition of class, and communitarians and multiculturalists relocate it in spheres and cultures — together showing that genuine equality is plural, not simple. Q — Discuss the dimensions of equality — legal, political, economic and social — and how they combine into formal and substantive equality. What it’s asking:  List the four working dimensions of equality, then show which two make ‘formal’ equality and which two make ‘substantive’ equality. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Legal equality  — rule of law plus ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.  (Equal rights are useless without equal power to vindicate them — hence free legal aid.) 2. Political equality  — ‘one person, one vote’ with no bar to office; yet  Lipson : ‘the many have always been governed by the few’.  (Every vote weighs the same, but money, birth and bureaucracy still weigh more.) 3. Economic equality  — a level playing field of access to wealth;  Tawney : it needs ‘the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’.  (Progressive taxation funding schools and health — Laski’s ‘problem of proportion’.) 4. Social equality  — ends discrimination by caste, creed, religion or sex, and is ‘enhanced by affirmative action’.  (Temple entry and common water sources, not merely an equal wage.) 5. Formal vs substantive  — the four dimensions combine into two.  (The queue.)    5.1 Formal  — legal + political.  (‘First come, first served’.)    5.2 Substantive  — social + economic.  (A separate line for the elderly and the disabled.) 6. Conclusion  — the welfare state’s task is to convert formal equality into substantive equality. Model Answer 1. Legal equality.  Legal equality grants equal legal status to all: the  rule of law , supplemented by ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.  Rousseau  regarded it as the primary mark of an equal society. Its limit is decisive: it is ‘meaningless without equal opportunity to get justice — all may possess equal rights but not equal power to vindicate them’, which is why free legal aid, not merely an open court, is required. 2. Political equality.  Political equality means equal political rights on a ‘one person, one vote’ basis, with no bar of birth or property to holding office.  Lipson  nevertheless notes that the ‘many have always been governed by the few’: political inequality has rested successively on knowledge ( Plato ), birth (aristocracy), money (plutocracy) and race, and real power may still vest in the bureaucracy, police and army rather than in the electorate. 3. Economic equality.  Economic equality seeks a ‘level playing field’ of access to wealth and the means of livelihood.  R.H. Tawney  insists that ‘equality of opportunity is not simply legal equality — it depends on the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’, so the state must actively build capacity.  Laski  adds that it is ‘a problem of proportion’, met through differential taxation and social expenditure rather than identical incomes. 4. Social equality.  Social equality ends discrimination on grounds of caste, creed, religion, sex and the like, attacking status hierarchy rather than income — the equal use of a temple, a well or a school matters as much as the equal wage. It is the dimension most resistant to legislation alone, which is why it is said to be ‘enhanced by affirmative action’. 5. Formal versus substantive.  The four dimensions combine into two composite forms, and the queue captures the difference exactly:    5.1 Formal  — “legal and political equality together form  formal equality ”; ‘first come, first served’ applies one rule to everybody.    5.2 Substantive  — “social and economic equality together form  substantive equality ”; a separate line for the elderly or the differently-abled relaxes the rule according to need. 6. Conclusion.  Formal equality supplies equal rules and equal votes; substantive equality supplies real, need-sensitive equality of condition — and the central task of the modern welfare state is to convert the former into the latter. Q — “Affirmative action is indispensable to substantive equality yet deeply contested.” Examine the arguments for and against it, with the Indian reservation debate. What it’s asking:  Define affirmative action, argue both sides, and settle the Indian reservation question with the courts’ test. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What it is  — ‘positive intervention by the state’ in favour of the historically disadvantaged.  (Reservation for SCs/STs in India, affirmative action for Blacks in the USA.) 2. Group-based, not individual  — the unit of claim is the community, not the person.  (A poor Brahmin does not qualify, since his community suffered no historical disadvantage — he is helped by poverty schemes instead.) 3. Arguments for  — it is the engine that turns formal equality into substantive equality:    3.1 Compensatory discrimination  — on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’, correcting unjust historical inequality.    3.2 Constitutional basis  — grounded in  Articles 15 and 16 . 4. Arguments against  —  neo-conservatives  object on four counts:    4.1 Erodes merit  — quotas ‘erode respect for merit’.    4.2 Offends procedural justice  — the already advantaged within a beneficiary group edge out poorer members of the majority.    4.3 Misplaced burden  — the present generation is ‘not responsible for past injustice’.    4.4 Wounds self-respect  — breeding a feeling of inferiority in those it is meant to lift. 5. The Indian debate  — critics and courts:    5.1 Guha  — it ‘generates more heat than light’.    5.2 Mehta  — ‘reservation makes us immoral’.    5.3 The courts  — enabling and temporary;  Ashok Kumar : ‘the medicine, not the daily bread’. 6. Conclusion  — indispensable, but legitimate only while it stays targeted, time-bound and evidence-based. Model Answer 1. What it is.  Affirmative action is ‘positive intervention by the state — welfare policies in favour of the disadvantaged’. It targets the  historically disadvantaged  — Dalits and Adivasis in India, Blacks in the United States — and works by relaxing a uniform rule (reserved seats, relaxed cut-offs, preferential appointment) so that those excluded for centuries can in fact enter. It must be distinguished from a mere  preferential policy  secured by already dominant groups, such as the Jat and Maratha agitations. 2. Group-based, not individual.  Its unit of claim is the  class or community, not the individual . A poor Brahmin does not qualify, because his community suffered no historical disadvantage — his poverty is addressed instead by income-based poverty-alleviation schemes. This is what distinguishes affirmative action from welfare simpliciter: it remedies a status injury inflicted on a group, not a shortfall of income suffered by a person. 3. Arguments for.  It is the engine by which formal equality is converted into substantive equality, and the case rests on two limbs:    3.1 Compensatory discrimination  — positive discrimination on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’, correcting  unjust historical inequalities  and enabling the deprived to ‘escape tough competition’ in which their starting handicap would be decisive.    3.2 Constitutional basis  — in India it is grounded in  Articles 15 and 16 , which permit special provision for socially and educationally backward classes. 4. Arguments against.  Neo-conservatives  hold that equality means only equality of opportunity, and press four objections:    4.1 Erodes merit  — quotas ‘erode respect for merit’.    4.2 Offends procedural justice  — it is ‘inimical to  procedural justice ’, since already advantaged members of a beneficiary group may edge out poorer members of the majority.    4.3 Misplaced burden  — the present generation is ‘not responsible for past injustice’, so the burden falls in the wrong place.    4.4 Wounds self-respect  — it injures  self-respect , breeding a ‘feeling of inferiority’ in those it is meant to lift. 5. The Indian debate.  Critics and courts have framed the Indian question in three voices:    5.1 Guha  —  Ramachandra Guha  observes that reservation debates ‘generate more heat than light’.    5.2 Mehta  —  Pratap Bhanu Mehta  charges that ‘reservation makes us immoral’.    5.3 The courts  — they have framed it as  enabling and temporary : in the  Ram Singh (Jat)  case the government was directed to keep identifying genuinely vulnerable classes on fresh evidence rather than political pressure, and in  Ashok Kumar  it was held that reservation is ‘the medicine, not the daily bread’ — a remedy for a diagnosed disability, not a permanent diet. 6. Conclusion.  Affirmative action is indispensable for converting formal into substantive equality, and is simply  Aristotle’s  rule that unequals be treated unequally. Its legitimacy, however, depends on its remaining  targeted, time-bound and evidence-based  — correcting a historical wrong without hardening into a permanent entitlement. Q — Is liberty a precondition for equality? Examine the relationship between liberty, equality and justice, and evaluate Berlin’s value pluralism. What it’s asking:  Take the liberty–equality relation through three schools, then test whether Berlin’s pluralism allows any final ranking. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The question  — liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’, and three schools read the relation differently.  (Does a quota that opens a college seat enlarge freedom or invade it?) 2. Libertarian  —  Hayek, Nozick : the two are contradictory, so liberty comes first and equality stops at law and opportunity.  (Redistribution means taxing one man to fund another.) 3. Socialist  — equality first, since ‘bourgeois’ liberty is a privilege of the propertied;  Hobhouse : ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. 4. Socio-liberal  — no necessary conflict; three routes.  (A literate voter is a freer voter.)    4.1 Rawls  — lexical order: equal basic liberties first, the difference principle after.    4.2 Dworkin  — endowment- and ambition-sensitive distribution.    4.3 Sen  — development as freedom. 5. Berlin’s value pluralism  — values are ‘plural, conflicting and incommensurable’, with no objective ordering.  (The goods of the nun’s life and the married woman’s are both real and cannot both be had.) 6. Conclusion  — liberty is a precondition only for  substantive  equality — ‘treating people as equals’; justice remains the balancing value. Model Answer 1. The question.  Liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’ values, and the practical form of the dispute is sharp: does a reserved seat or a redistributive tax enlarge the freedom of the excluded, or invade the freedom of the taxed? Three schools answer differently, according to whether they treat the two values as contradictory, as hierarchically ordered, or as mutually completing. 2. Libertarian.  Libertarians and classical liberals ( Locke, Smith, Bentham, Nozick, Hayek ) hold liberty and equality to be  contradictory , give liberty priority, and confine equality to legal equality and equality of opportunity, since redistribution means coercing one person for another’s benefit.  Hayek : ‘people are very different, so treating them equally must produce inequality; equality before law leads to material inequality’ — a result he accepts as the price of freedom. 3. Socialist.  Socialists and Marxists reverse the order: equality trumps a merely ‘bourgeois’ liberty, because without material equality freedom is the privilege of the propertied — the right to own a newspaper means nothing to one who cannot buy one.  Hobhouse  states the point decisively: ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. 4. Socio-liberal.  Socio-liberals and egalitarians ( Rawls, Sen, Dworkin ) deny any necessary conflict, by three distinct routes:    4.1 Rawls  — he reconciles them in  lexical order , the equal basic liberties ranking first and the difference principle governing what remains.    4.2 Dworkin  — he does so through endowment- and ambition-sensitive distribution.    4.3 Sen  — through ‘development as freedom’, since literacy, health and nutrition are what make a formal right usable. On this view liberty, properly understood, is a precondition of a meaningful equal life, not its enemy. 5. Berlin’s value pluralism.  Isaiah Berlin  argues that fundamental values are ‘universal, plural, conflicting and incommensurable’ — ‘there is no objective criterion to determine their ordering’, as the goods realised in the life of a nun and in that of a married woman are both genuine and cannot both be possessed. He rejects value monism, which assumes one true ranking, and equally value relativism, which denies that values are real: liberty and equality are both authentic goods that may irreducibly clash. 6. Conclusion.  Liberty is a precondition for equality only when equality is understood  substantively  — as ‘treating people as equals’ with equal concern and respect, rather than treating them identically.  Berlin’s  pluralism warns that no single formula can always harmonise them, which is precisely why justice, as the balancing value, remains the central task of political theory. Q — “Aristotle supports proportionate, not absolute, equality.” Discuss his conception of equality and its relevance to modern substantive equality. What it’s asking:  Explain what proportional equality means in Aristotle, note its limits in his own society, and show it is the logic of affirmative action today. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Proportional, not arithmetical  —  Politics : ‘the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’.  (Equal marks deserve equal grades; unequal need deserves unequal help.) 2. Injustice runs both ways  — ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’.  (One flight of stairs for everyone is equal treatment that excludes the wheelchair user.) 3. Desert and proportion  — in distributive justice, honours and wealth go by relevant merit, not identical division; hence  absolute or mechanical equality  is rejected. 4. Its limits  — proportionality is only as just as its criteria of relevance:    4.1 Natural inequality accepted  — he ranked citizens above slaves and men above women in ‘rational and civic capacity’.    4.2 Yet inequality breeds revolution  — ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’. 5. Relevance  — ‘unequals treated unequally’ is the very logic of  substantive equality :    5.1 Reservation  — under Articles 15–16.    5.2 Progressive taxation  — unequal rates for unequal incomes.    5.3 Special provision  — for the disabled, and a separate queue for the elderly — all relax a uniform rule for the disadvantaged. 6. Conclusion  — though framed in a hierarchical Greek polis, his proportionality is the enduring premise of the welfare state. Model Answer 1. Proportional, not arithmetical.  Aristotle’s  conception of equality is  proportional, not arithmetical . In the  Politics  he defines just equality as “the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” Equality is thus a ratio, not a quantity: what is owed to a person depends on the relevant respect in which he stands equal or unequal to others, so identical treatment is just only among genuine equals. 2. Injustice runs both ways.  From this follows his most quoted proposition: ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’. The second half is the radical half — a single flight of stairs applied to everyone alike is impeccably equal treatment which nonetheless excludes the person in a wheelchair. Uniformity, in other words, can itself be a form of injustice. 3. Desert and proportion.  Equality therefore becomes a matter of  desert and proportion : in distributive justice, honours, office and wealth are to be shared according to relevant merit rather than divided identically, and the argument turns on which respects are relevant to which good. He accordingly rejects  absolute or mechanical equality  as itself a source of injustice — the objection later pressed by  Hayek  against equality of outcome. 4. Its limits.  Proportionality is only as just as the criteria of relevance it employs, and Aristotle’s own criteria were severely limited:    4.1 Natural inequality accepted  — he distinguished citizens from slaves and men from women in ‘rational and civic capacity’, restricted participation in the Polis to citizens, and even held slavery to be ‘good for both master and slave’.    4.2 Yet inequality breeds revolution  — he was acutely alert to inequality’s dangers: ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’. 5. Relevance.  His principle that ‘unequals be treated unequally’ is precisely the logic of modern  substantive equality  and  affirmative action , each instance relaxing a uniform rule in favour of the disadvantaged:    5.1 Reservation  — under Articles 15 and 16 of the Indian Constitution.    5.2 Progressive taxation  — unequal rates levied on unequal incomes.    5.3 Special provision  — special provisions for the disabled and a separate queue for the elderly, treating unequals unequally so as to produce genuine rather than merely formal equality. 6. Conclusion.  Aristotle’s proportional equality, though embedded in a hierarchical Greek society, supplies the enduring insight behind today’s welfare state — that real equality often requires differential, need-sensitive treatment rather than identical treatment for all.
